## Goals

-   Know when parametric assumptions are too badly violated to trust
-   Fit common nonparametric alternatives to the tests from this course
-   Get a brief look at permutation tests as a general-purpose backup

## Setup



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
```
:::



## When parametric tests break down

Recall from Labs 4–6: t-tests, ANOVA, and regression all assume roughly normal, equal-variance residuals. When sample sizes are small and that assumption clearly fails (e.g., strongly skewed data, extreme outliers you can't justify removing), nonparametric methods based on ranks are a safer choice.

## Wilcoxon rank-sum test (nonparametric alternative to the t-test)



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data(sleep)
wilcox.test(extra ~ group, data = sleep)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  extra by group
W = 25.5, p-value = 0.06933
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
```


:::
:::



Compare to the parametric version from Week 7's tutorial:



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
t.test(extra ~ group, data = sleep)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  extra by group
t = -1.8608, df = 17.776, p-value = 0.07939
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 1 and group 2 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -3.3654832  0.2054832
sample estimates:
mean in group 1 mean in group 2 
           0.75            2.33 
```


:::
:::



::: callout-note
## Exercise 1

The conclusions here happen to roughly agree. In general, why might a Wilcoxon test and a t-test disagree on a dataset with a small sample and a couple of extreme outliers? Which test is more sensitive to those outliers, and why?
:::

## Kruskal-Wallis test (nonparametric alternative to one-way ANOVA)



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data(PlantGrowth)
kruskal.test(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  weight by group
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 7.9882, df = 2, p-value = 0.01842
```


:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Parametric version from Week 7's tutorial, for comparison
summary(aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
group        2  3.766  1.8832   4.846 0.0159 *
Residuals   27 10.492  0.3886                 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
```


:::
:::



## Spearman correlation (nonparametric alternative to Pearson)



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data(trees)
cor.test(trees$Girth, trees$Volume, method = "spearman")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  trees$Girth and trees$Volume
S = 224.61, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
      rho 
0.9547151 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
cor.test(trees$Girth, trees$Volume, method = "pearson")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  trees$Girth and trees$Volume
t = 20.478, df = 29, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.9322519 0.9841887
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.9671194 
```


:::
:::



::: callout-note
## Exercise 2

Spearman correlation is based on ranks rather than raw values. Name one situation where Spearman would be clearly preferable to Pearson (think about the shape of the relationship, not just outliers).
:::

## A general-purpose backup: permutation test

When no standard nonparametric test fits your design, a permutation test lets you build a null distribution directly from your data.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(99)
observed_diff <- PlantGrowth |>
  filter(group %in% c("trt1", "trt2")) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(m = mean(weight)) |>
  summarise(diff = diff(m)) |>
  pull(diff)

perm_data <- PlantGrowth |> filter(group %in% c("trt1", "trt2"))

n_perm <- 2000
perm_diffs <- replicate(n_perm, {
  shuffled <- sample(perm_data$group)
  perm_data |>
    mutate(group = shuffled) |>
    group_by(group) |>
    summarise(m = mean(weight), .groups = "drop") |>
    summarise(diff = diff(m)) |>
    pull(diff)
})

p_value <- mean(abs(perm_diffs) >= abs(observed_diff))
p_value
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.008
```


:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tibble(diff = perm_diffs) |>
  ggplot(aes(diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_diff, color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Permuted mean difference (trt2 - trt1)",
       title = "Red line = observed difference") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Permutation null distribution with observed difference](week14-tutorial_files/figure-html/fig-perm-1.png){#fig-perm width=672}
:::
:::



::: callout-note
## Exercise 3

Compare the permutation p-value to a standard `t.test()` p-value on the same two groups (`trt1` vs. `trt2` in `PlantGrowth`). Are they similar? In your own words, explain what the permutation test is doing conceptually — what does "shuffling `group`" simulate under the null hypothesis?
:::
